title: the sound the universe hums
hook: the sound a room makes together; it's three sounds and a silence
tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do

segments.voice: Yesterday, namaste: I bow to you. Your line was the light in me sees the light in you. Did you see anyone that way, even once? It counts either way. Day two.

A room goes quiet. Someone at the front takes a slow breath, and then everyone makes the same long sound together, strangers on their mats, for a few seconds. Om. Then the mats get rolled up and nobody mentions it. Some people feel a little self-conscious making that sound. Fair enough. But the syllable has a whole old text built around it, and that text doesn't treat it as one sound. It hears three sounds inside it, and then a fourth part that isn't a sound at all. You can feel all of it in your own mouth in a single breath. Today, what om is made of.
screen: `A ROOM, ONE SOUND.` → `OM.` → `THREE SOUNDS, AND A FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Say it slowly and feel where it lives. Aaa: the mouth wide open, the sound at the back of the throat. Uuu: the lips round, and the sound moves forward. Mmm: the lips close, and the hum sits in the front of your face. Open, middle, closed. That's why it's sometimes written aum. The text I mentioned is the Mandukya Upanishad. It opens with a big claim: om is all of this. All that was, all that is, all that will be, and whatever lies beyond time too. Then it does something careful. It gives each sound a state of being. A is waking: the world of things you can see and touch. U is dreaming: the inner world, made of the mind. M is deep, dreamless sleep, where everything goes quiet and nothing is wanted. Three sounds, three states a person passes through in an ordinary day. And then the fourth. The Upanishad calls it simply the fourth. It has no sound. It's the silence after the mmm runs out, and the text says that silence is the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away. So om isn't a sign-off. It's a map. Everything you go through in a day, in one breath, and then the quiet under all of it. Om is said at the start of prayers and readings. The Bhagavad Gita says that acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with it. A first sound, before the words.
screen: `A — WAKING.` · `U — DREAMING.` · `M — DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH — THE SILENCE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING, IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. If you're somewhere you can't make a sound, hum it inside; it works the same. Sit up a little. Breathe in, all the way. Now, slowly, let it out as the sound: aaa, uuu, mmm. Let the mmm go until it runs out on its own. And then don't do anything. Just notice the quiet that's left. That's the fourth part.
Om. Three sounds for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and a silence for the fourth. Everything, in one breath. Second word on your strand, next to namaste.
screen: `OM — your 2nd word` → clicks onto the strand beside namaste.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: one sound, before words. Once today, before you say something that matters, a text, a call, a hard sentence, take one breath first. That's all. Day two.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THING THAT'S YOURS TO DO.`

howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

match.prompt: what's inside the sound — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: the Mandukya Upanishad gives a to waking, u to dreaming and m to deep sleep. what does it give the fourth part?
fork.reveal: the fourth has no sound at all. the text calls it the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away.

original.note: Sanskrit: the sacred syllable, written as one sign. the Mandukya Upanishad hears a, u and m inside it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hum to end a yoga class.
what it means: three sounds and a silence, the whole of a day in one breath.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya Upanishad: a for waking, u for dream, m for deep sleep, and the soundless fourth, called simply the fourth (chaturtha; later teachers call it turiya).

notes: Mandukya verse 1 (om is all this: past, present, future, and beyond the three times) and verses 8–12 (a, u, m as waking, dream, deep sleep; the soundless fourth, peaceful, the self) are paraphrased. Confirm verse numbers and that 'the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away' fairly renders verse 12 (prapanchopashama, shiva, advaita).
Gita 17.24 says that for those who follow Vedic teaching, acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity begin with om; paraphrased as 'offering, giving and discipline'. Confirm.
Cut from manuscript day 2 under the claims rule: 'every yoga class on earth', 'the most-analyzed syllable in human history', the Mandukya being 'about eight hundred words' and 'one of the shortest'.
Title keeps the index ('the sound the universe hums'); the script doesn't claim the universe literally hums. Keeper may want a line on how tradition speaks of om as the primal sound.

Editor pass: hook no longer tells the listener they felt self-conscious ('some people feel'); 'in about ten seconds' cut to 'in a single breath' under the claims rule; Mandukya ref widened to 1, 3–5, 7–12, since the states (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth) are described in 3–5 and 7 and mapped to a, u, m and the soundless fourth in 8–12.

Editor review 2: trapdoor said the Mandukya calls the fourth 'turiya'; the Mandukya's own word is chaturtha (verses 7, 12), and turiya is the later term (Gaudapada and others), so the floor now says both. Spoken lines read and left as they were.
